'''George Edward Pake''' (April 1, 1924 &ndash; March 4, 2004) was a physicist, academic, and research executive primarily known for helping found [[Xerox PARC]].

== Early life ==
Pake was raised in [[Kent, Ohio]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=George Pake - National Academy of Sciences |url=https://www.nasonline.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/pake-george.pdf}}</ref> His father was an English instructor at [[Kent State University]].<ref name="NASPDF">{{cite web 
|title= ''George Edward Pake 1924—2004'' |first= Charles P. |last= Slichter
|url=https://www.nasonline.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/pake-george.pdf|publisher= National Academy of Sciences |location= Washington, D.C.
|website = www.nasonline.org |date= 2009 | access-date = September 11, 2025}}</ref>{{rp|3}} His mother was a schoolteacher.{{citation needed|date=January 2018}}

Pake was exempted from service in the [[United States Armed Forces]] during World War II due to [[scoliosis]]. He earned bachelor's and master's degrees from the [[Carnegie Institute of Technology]] and his doctorate in physics at [[Harvard University]] in 1948.

== Career ==
Much of his early research at Harvard University focused on the topic of [[Nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy|nuclear magnetic resonance]] (NMR) spectroscopy. There, he discovered the multiplet structure produced by the dipolar coupling of two nuclear spins.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Pake |first=G. E. |date=April 1948 |title=Nuclear Resonance Absorption in Hydrated Crystals: Fine Structure of the Proton Line |url=http://aip.scitation.org/doi/10.1063/1.1746878 |journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics |language=en |volume=16 |issue=4 |pages=327–336 |doi=10.1063/1.1746878 |bibcode=1948JChPh..16..327P |issn=0021-9606|url-access=subscription }}</ref> In his honor, this multiplet is now known as the [[Pake doublet]] and forms the basis for NMR-based inter-atomic distance measurements and molecular structure determination.

After four years as a [[physics]] professor at [[Washington University in St. Louis]], Pake became the head of the physics department at age 28.<ref name="GEPObNYT">{{cite web 
| first = John
| last = Markoff
| title = George Pake, Computer Pioneer, Dies at 79 
| url = https://www.nytimes.com/2004/03/11/us/george-pake-computer-pioneer-dies-at-79.html
| website = [[The New York Times]]
| date = March 11, 2004
| access-date = January 17, 2018}}</ref> He later went on to become provost of the university from 1962 to 1970 before leaving to serve as founding director of [[Xerox PARC]].

Pake served on the [[President's Science Advisory Committee]] (1965-1969).<ref name="Niels Bohr Library & Archives">{{cite web | title=United States. President's Science Advisory Committee | website=Niels Bohr Library & Archives | url=https://history.aip.org/phn/21612015.html | access-date=1 August 2018}}</ref> He was president of the [[American Physical Society]] in 1977.

PARC assembled a first-rate collection of research talent, especially in the area of computer science. During Pake's years running Xerox PARC, the research center invented the [[laser printer]] and pioneered the use of a computer "desktop" which functioned by clicking on "icons." 
This has since become the computer industry standard.

Despite advocacy by Pake, the [[Xerox|Xerox Corporation]] never chose to open a personal computer division. Pake left Xerox in 1986 to direct the nonprofit [[Institute for Research on Learning]] in Palo Alto.<ref name="GEPObLAT">{{cite web 
| first = Alex
| last = Pham
| title = George E. Pake, 79; Physicist Directed Xerox's Famous Palo Alto Research Center
| url = https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2004-mar-11-me-pake11-story.html
| website = [[Los Angeles Times]]
| date = March 11, 2004
| access-date = January 17, 2018}}</ref> He remained director emeritus until the time of his death.<ref name="GEPObInd">{{cite web 
| title = George Pake Godfather of the computer revolution
| url = https://www.independent.co.uk/news/obituaries/george-pake-38172.html
| publisher = The Independent
| website = www.independent.co.uk
| date = March 15, 2004
| access-date = January 17, 2018}}</ref>

Late in life, Pake began writing two different books, both with the collaborator [[Andrew Szanton]]. Pake's death, of heart failure on March 4, 2004, in [[Tucson, Arizona]], interrupted both book projects.

== Awards ==
In 1986, Pake was awarded the [[IRI Medal]] from the [[Industrial Research Institute]] for recognition of his leadership in the field of technology and innovation. Pake was also a recipient of the [[National Medal of Science]] in 1987 and continued to visit PARC long after his 1986 retirement from Xerox.

== George E. Pake Prize ==
Since 1984, the [[American Physical Society]] has been awarding the George E. Pake Prize, endowed in 1983 by the Xerox Corporation, to recognize outstanding work by physicists combining original research accomplishments with leadership in the management of research or development in industry.<ref name="GEPPrize_APS">{{cite web 
| title = George E. Pake Prize
| url = https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/pake.cfm
| publisher = American Physical Society
| website = www.aps.org
| date = 2018
| access-date = January 17, 2018}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
Pake married Marjorie Semon on May 31, 1947; they had four children.<ref name="NASPDF"/>{{rp|20}}
